meta.title: Who really said "The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — King wrote it. "The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind" is in Stride Toward Freedom (1958), p. 213. The Gandhi version has no source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind'?
meta.ogDescription: King really did write this line, in Stride Toward Freedom (1958). But the famous Gandhi version of the aphorism has no Gandhi source — and dates to 1914.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister and civil rights leader
answer.sourceLine: This exact sentence appears in King’s first book, Stride Toward Freedom: The Montgomery Story, published by Harper & Brothers and released on 17 September 1958; Quote Investigator cites it to page 213 ↗. The idea is older than King, and the better-known “makes the whole world blind” version pinned on Gandhi has never been traced to Gandhi at all.

source.excerpt: The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind.
trail: Quote Investigator’s study of the aphorism ↗ quotes King’s sentence in full and cites it to page 213 of Stride Toward Freedom: The Montgomery Story (1958).
The Stanford King Institute’s entry on the book ↗ records that King signed with Harper & Brothers in October 1957 and that the book “was officially released on 17 September 1958.”
A 1958 Harper printing is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗, listing publisher “New York, Harper” and date 1958.
Wikiquote lists the saying under “Misattributed” on its Gandhi page ↗, and its dated chronology includes the 1958 King wording alongside the 1914, 1950 and 1982 citations.
source.excerptNote: The sentence sits inside King’s case against retaliatory violence, which he calls “both impractical and immoral” — impractical because, in his argument, it spirals downward into destruction for everyone; immoral because it seeks to humiliate an opponent rather than win him over. Stride Toward Freedom is King’s memoir of the Montgomery bus boycott. The passage is quoted in full by Quote Investigator ↗.

The Stanford King Institute ↗ states that it “cannot give permission to use or reproduce any of the writings” of King and directs requests to Intellectual Properties Management, “the exclusive licensor of the Estate of Martin Luther King, Jr., Inc.” A current in-print edition is issued by Beacon Press in the King Legacy series ↗.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.metaLine: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and the most prominent leader of the civil rights movement from 1955 until his assassination in 1968, advancing civil rights through nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience against Jim Crow laws and other forms of legalised discrimination. Stride Toward Freedom: The Montgomery Story (1958) was his first book, an account of the Montgomery bus boycott that doubled as his first full statement of the philosophy behind it. Because his name is among the most quoted in English, it is also among the most falsely quoted — which makes the genuinely sourced lines, like this one, worth marking as sourced.

misattribution.heading: The tangle around this line
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a King quotation, the words really are his. The confusion runs the other way: the aphorism King was reworking is one of the most misattributed sayings on the internet, and the version most people can recite belongs to neither King nor the man it is credited to.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that no example of Gandhi using the saying has ever been discovered, and that the Yale Book of Quotations records only a second-hand belief, via the Gandhi Institute for Nonviolence, that the family thinks it authentic — with no year, place or work attached. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗.

items.scope: How Gandhi came to get the credit
items.why: Fischer used the image twice while describing Gandhi’s philosophy — “an ‘eye for an eye’ which, in the end, would make everybody blind” in Gandhi and Stalin (1947), and a version in The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) — but did not attribute the words to Gandhi ↗. Quote Investigator suggests Fischer’s books may have inadvertently helped establish the misattribution.

items.scope: The line most people can actually recite
items.who: John Briley, screenwriter of the 1982 film Gandhi
items.why: The Oscar-winning biopic put “An eye for an eye only ends up making the whole world blind” into Gandhi’s mouth, which Quote Investigator credits with popularising the association ↗. Wikiquote cites a 1993 Michigan Today profile of Briley by Jon Krampner ↗ reporting that Gandhi never said it and that Briley wrote the words.

Aggregators circulate “That old law about ‘an eye for an eye’ leaves everybody blind. The time is always right to do the right thing” as one King quotation — as Quotefancy does, with no source given ↗. That is a reworded first half welded to a separate King sentence; the published book reads “The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind.”

misattribution.truthLine: King wrote it, in 1958, in his own book — but he was reworking an image already in circulation: the earliest form located by Quote Investigator ↗ is from Canadian MP George Perry Graham, arguing against capital punishment in the House of Commons on 5 February 1914.

context.heading: Why King reached for it
lead: Stride Toward Freedom was King’s account of the Montgomery bus boycott, written while the movement was still young and, in the King Institute’s telling ↗, produced against publishing deadlines with significant guidance from Stanley Levison, Bayard Rustin and Harris Wofford. The book lays out three ways oppressed people meet oppression — acquiescence, violence, and nonviolent resistance — and this sentence is the hinge of the argument against the second.

The phrasing matters. King does not say revenge is wrong because it is unkind; he says the arithmetic of reciprocal harm does not close. It is an argument about outcomes aimed at people who thought nonviolence was naive, which is why he pairs “impractical” with “immoral” rather than leading with the moral claim.
detailsBody: King was deeply read in Gandhian thought — the King Institute notes that the book’s “Pilgrimage to Nonviolence” chapter works through the influence of Thoreau, Marx, Aristotle, Rauschenbusch and Gandhi on his thinking. That lineage is real, and it is part of why the aphorism and the two men became fused in popular memory.

But influence is not authorship. The documented chain runs: a 1914 parliamentary flourish, a biographer’s 1947 and 1950 paraphrases of Gandhi’s philosophy, King’s own 1958 sentence, and a 1982 screenplay line — and only one link in that chain is a named author saying it in his own published book.
context.pull: Everyone remembers the Gandhi version. The sourced version is King’s.
